title: Characterizing the Trainability of Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial Circuit Born Machines
claim: Gradient variance collapses exponentially with system size for dense or high-weight settings, which predicts whether training succeeds; sparse structures stay trainable.
layout: 2x3 grid of plots; top gradient scaling, bottom training curves per architecture
description: Two rows of three line plots. The top row shows the estimated variance of the MMD loss derivative on a log y-axis against qubit count (20 to 200). Each panel uses a different kernel frequency weight: |a|=2, ceil(log n), and n/4. Five dashed, colored curves with error bars are shown: Product (blue), Sparse ER c=0.5 (green), Sparse ER c=2 (yellow), 2D Lattice (purple) and Complete (red). They fall at very different rates, and the red and yellow curves hit the floor first. The bottom row shows training loss against iteration on a log scale for 2D Lattice, Sparse ER and Complete circuits. Lines are colored by sample size (64 to 1024) with shaded noise bands. The Lattice loss drops clearly, Sparse ER drops only with large samples, and Complete stays flat. Legends sit in the top-right and bottom-right panels.
caption: Top: Scaling of the MMD derivative with respect to the number of qubits, measured on MNIST-inspired datasets and reporting the mean and standard deviation over $50$ repetitions. Bottom: Trajectories of the MMD training loss for learning the $784$-qubit binarized MNIST dataset, with increasing sample sizes for estimating the MMD loss.
abstract: Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial Circuit Born Machines (IQP-QCBMs) have been proposed as quantum generative models that combine a classically tractable training objective - based on the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) - with a potential quantum advantage motivated by sampling-complexity arguments. While recent works have explored this model across various application domains, fundamental questions remain: does the model suffer from exponentially vanishing loss gradients, known as the barren plateau problem - a pervasive obstacle in quantum machine learning - and how do regimes of trainability relate to regimes of possible quantum advantage? Here, we address both questions analytically. To study trainability, we derive closed-form expressions for the variances of the partial derivatives of the MMD loss function and establish general upper and lower bounds. We explicitly characterize how trainability depends on the generator set and the spectrum of the chosen kernel, identifying regimes in which low Hamming-weight kernels avoid exponential gradient suppression under structured topologies. Regarding potential quantum advantage, we reformulate the anti-concentration property in terms of the same generator-set quantities that govern trainability, enabling a unified analysis. We show that sparse IQP architectures can produce classically intractable output distributions while simultaneously remaining trainable, at least at lower-weight frequencies. Our analytical results corroborate the numerical observations of prior work and provide principled guidelines for designing scalable IQP-QCBM architectures.
